Indie devs and publishers hit in Gamescom equipment thefts
Thieves obtained access to Gamescom's Indie Arena and business area and stole a number of laptops and Steam Decks from smaller exhibitors.
Bryant Francis
,
Senior Editor
,
GameDeveloper.com
August 31, 2026
2 Min Read
Image via Gamescom
A number of independent developers and publishers suffered a frustrating end to their Gamescom trips last week after arriving to the show floor on Friday and discovering thieves had stolen a number of locked-up laptops and Steam Decks from their booths. Now show organizers are facing questions from developers asking if the event did enough to prevent security breaches.
Word of the thefts began spreading after
Mimic
developer Ryan Laley
posted a video on X stating
that his and others' laptops had been stolen from Gamescom's business area the night before. Publisher and event organizer iam8bit
also reported its hardware
was stolen from the same area. Meanwhile, developer
Tessera Studios
reported that two laptops and a Steam Deck were stolen from their booth in the Indie Arena (hosted in a separate region of Gamescom convention hall Koelnmesse). They said the laptops contained "personal, company, and critical information."
Related:
Housemarque co-founder Ilari Kuittinen exits from studio
The game industry responded to these thefts with words and offerings of support for the affected developers—and a slew of questions for Gamescom management.
Cyberpunk 2
and
The Witcher 4
developer CD Projekt Red responded to Laley with
an offer of new hardware
to replace his stolen gear, and Games From Spain
swooped in
to help the Tessera Studios team continue showcasing their game.
On Saturday, Gamescom's organizers posted a statement on X following "many requests" for information about the thefts, where it described its general security practices and expressed sadness for the impacted independent developers. "Uniformed guards provide general security across the venue. Individual stand security can be booked separately, and exhibitors are advised to insure equipment against theft," the organizers wrote. "This is noted in the terms and conditions of participation and the technical guidelines."
Industry professionals
expressed frustration
over this response, with some saying that this isn't the first year developers have been robbed at the event. Australian publisher Ukiyo Studios did not report any equipment stolen this year, but
posted
that they had been "blocked" from filing a police report by Gamescom organizers after a PC was stolen from its booth in 2024. The publisher said they had been told that such a report could make the event and city of Cologne "look bad."
It does appear that event organizers are keeping in touch with impacted developers, as Laley
has posted
that he "had the pleasure" of speaking with one of Gamescom's directors on Sunday. In its statement, the event did stress that security is one of organizers' "highest priorities," and that its measures are designed to minimize the risks of "individuals attempting to take advantage of the situation" surrounding security at an event of this size.
Related:

Game Developer has reached out to Gamescom and Koelnmesse for comment on Ukiyo Studios' claim concerning the blocked police report. We will update this story upon response from the organizers.
